title: Percentages for Grade 5 Made Simple (Percent of a Number, the Easy Way) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Percentages Grade 5 Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach percentages grade 5 the clear way: percent as out of 100, fraction-decimal-percent swaps and finding a percent of a number, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: Percent just means out of 100 — and once a Grade 5 child sees that, finding 25% of 80 or 10% of a bill stops being scary. Here is how I teach it, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Show a Grade 5 class a shirt marked ‘25% off’ and half of them will guess the discount is ₹25, no matter what the shirt costs. That single mix-up is the whole reason percentages for grade 5 need to start not with tricks but with one plain idea: percent means ‘out of 100’. The little % sign is shorthand for ‘per hundred’. Once a child truly believes that 25% is just 25 out of every 100, everything else — converting fractions, reading a decimal, working out a discount — becomes a set of small, sensible steps instead of magic.

This is usually the first year children meet percentages formally in the NCERT sequence, so the goal is understanding, not speed. Give me a child who can explain why 50% is half over one who can rattle off answers but freezes at a real shop. Below is the order I teach it in, with the two skills that matter most at this stage: swapping between fractions, decimals and percentages, and finding a simple percentage of a quantity.

Percent means out of 100 — start here

Draw a 10 by 10 grid, one hundred little squares. Shade 25 of them. That shaded part is 25%. Shade half the grid and you have shaded 50 squares, which is 50%. I keep this grid on the board for a whole week because it quietly answers the questions that trip children up later: 100% is the full grid, and you cannot normally shade more than the whole thing, so most everyday percentages sit between 0 and 100.

The grid also makes the shortcut answers obvious. Ten squares in a column is 10%. One square is 1%. Children who picture the grid rarely make the ‘25% off means ₹25’ mistake, because they can see that 25% of a big number is big and 25% of a small number is small.

Converting fractions, decimals and percentages

Here is the honest truth: fractions, decimals and percentages are three costumes for the same number. Half can dress up as ½, as 0.5, or as 50%. Teaching the swaps is mostly teaching children to spot the same value wearing different clothes.

  • Fraction to percent: make the bottom number 100 if you can. ½ = 50/100 = 50%. ¼ = 25/100 = 25%. If you cannot get to 100 neatly, divide top by bottom and multiply by 100.
  • Decimal to percent: multiply by 100, which just slides the point two places right. 0.3 becomes 30%. 0.07 becomes 7%.
  • Percent to decimal: divide by 100, sliding the point two places left. 45% becomes 0.45.
  • Percent to fraction: write it over 100 and simplify. 20% = 20/100 = ⅕.

The equivalents worth knowing by heart are few, and I make children learn exactly these — they cover most of what school and shopping throw at them.

Finding a percentage of a quantity

This is the skill that pays off at the shop, and it rests on one rule: ‘of’ means multiply. To find 25% of 80, turn 25% into ¼ (or 0.25) and take a quarter of 80, which is 20. That is it. No formula sheet needed.

The 10% shortcut every child should own

Ten percent of any number is just that number with the decimal point moved one place left — you drop a zero, in effect. 10% of 80 is 8. 10% of 250 is 25. This one shortcut unlocks a whole toolkit:

  • 5% is half of 10%. So 5% of 80 is half of 8, which is 4.
  • 20% is double 10%. So 20% of 80 is 16.
  • 15% is 10% plus 5%. So 15% of 80 is 8 + 4 = 12.

I teach the 10% hop before any ‘proper’ method because it lets a ten-year-old estimate a restaurant tip or a sale price in their head, and that real-world win is what makes percentages stick.

Marks, discounts and Indian shopping

Percentages only feel real when they buy something. A few contexts I use every year with my students:

  • Marks: a child scoring 18 out of 20 has 18/20 = 90/100 = 90%. Report cards speak in percentages, so this one lands fast.
  • Discounts: a ₹600 pair of shoes at 25% off. The discount is ¼ of 600 = ₹150, so you pay ₹450. Notice we found the discount first, then subtracted — a common trip-up is forgetting the second step.
  • Festival sales: ‘10% off’ on a ₹1200 kurta is ₹120 saved. The 10% shortcut makes this a mental-maths question, not a calculator one.

One caveat I always flag: a bigger percentage is not always a bigger saving. 50% off a ₹200 toy saves ₹100; 20% off a ₹1000 cricket bat saves ₹200. The percentage and the price both matter, and spotting that is a genuinely useful bit of number sense for a Grade 5 child heading into a Diwali sale.

quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on percent as out of 100, converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, and finding a percentage of a number. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 percentages: basics and percent of a quantity

questions.q: What does the percent sign (%) mean?
questions.explanation: Percent means 'per hundred', so a percentage is a count out of 100. 25% is 25 out of every 100.

questions.q: Which percentage is the same as the fraction ½?

questions.explanation: To turn a decimal into a percent, multiply by 100 (move the point two places right). 0.3 becomes 30%.
10% of a number is that number with the decimal point moved one place left. 10% of 250 is 25.
25% is ¼, so take a quarter of 80. 80 divided by 4 is 20.
To turn a percent into a decimal, divide by 100 (move the point two places left). 45% becomes 0.45.

questions.q: A pair of shoes costs ₹600. In a 25% off sale, how much is the discount?
questions.explanation: 25% is ¼. A quarter of 600 is 150, so the discount is ₹150 (you would then pay ₹450).

questions.q: Riya scored 18 out of 20 in a test. What is her percentage?
questions.explanation: 18 out of 20 is the same as 90 out of 100, because 18/20 = 90/100. So she scored 90%.

faq.a: A percentage is a way of writing a number as a count out of 100. In Grade 5 children learn that percent means 'per hundred', how to swap between fractions, decimals and percentages, and how to find a simple percentage of a quantity like 25% of 80.

faq.q: How do you convert a fraction to a percentage?
faq.a: Make the bottom number 100 if you can, and the top number is the percentage. ½ = 50/100 = 50%, and ¼ = 25/100 = 25%. If you cannot reach 100 neatly, divide the top by the bottom and multiply the result by 100.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to find a percentage of a number?
faq.a: Start with 10%, which is just the number with its decimal point moved one place left — 10% of 80 is 8. From there, 5% is half of that, 20% is double, and 15% is 10% plus 5%. This mental-maths ladder handles most everyday percentages.

faq.q: Why do children mix up discounts and prices?
faq.a: Because they hear '25% off' and picture a fixed rupee amount instead of a fraction of the price. Teaching that a percentage depends on the number it is taken from — 25% of ₹600 is ₹150, not ₹25 — fixes this quickly.
